events.title: Antony withdraws to the desert fort of Pispir
events.summary: About 285 the Coptic-speaking farmer Antony, who had given away his inheritance c. 270 after hearing Matthew 19:21 read in church, shut himself in an abandoned fort at Pispir for some twenty years, emerging c. 305 to organise disciples; c. 313 he moved to the "Inner Mountain" near the Red Sea, where the Monastery of St Antony still stands. Athanasius' Life made him the model of the solitary monk.
events.locName: Pispir (Outer Mountain), east bank of the Nile
events.debate: Chronology rests on the Life of Antony; Antony's seven Coptic letters show a more learned figure than Athanasius portrays.

events.title: Maximian campaigns beyond the Rhine
events.summary: In 287 Maximian crossed the Rhine and ravaged Alamannic and Burgundian territory, while Diocletian advanced from Raetia; the panegyric of 289 hails it as the first Roman offensive beyond the river in a generation, and Maximian repelled raiders who attacked Gaul on 1 January 287 as he took up his consulship at Trier.

events.title: Diocletian's settlement with Bahram II
events.summary: Weakened by the revolt of his brother Hormizd in the east, Bahram II sent gifts to Diocletian, who claimed a diplomatic victory (Persicus Maximus) and restored the Arsacid Tiridates III to part of Armenia with Roman backing.

events.title: The Frankish king Gennobaudes receives his kingdom from Maximian
events.summary: Maximian forced Frankish groups on the lower Rhine to submit; their king Gennobaudes "received his kingdom" as a gift from the emperor, and Franks were settled in Roman territory as laeti, the beginning of an enduring Frankish presence in Toxandria and the lower Rhine.

events.title: Diocletian and Maximian meet at Milan
events.summary: In midwinter 290-291 the two Augusti crossed the Alps from Sirmium and Gaul to meet at Milan, appearing together in a staged adventus that the panegyric of 291 describes as a near-epiphany of Jupiter and Hercules. The meeting probably planned the Tetrarchy and the campaign against Carausius.

events.title: First mention of the Tervingi and Gepids
events.summary: The panegyric delivered to Maximian in 291 mentions the Tervingi, "another division of the Goths", fighting Vandals and Gepids, the first appearance of the Tervingi name. The orator presents barbarian infighting as a gift of the emperors' good fortune.

events.title: Galerius suppresses revolt at Coptos and Busiris
events.summary: Before the Persian war Galerius put down unrest in Egypt; Eusebius' Chronicle (via Jerome) records that Busiris and Coptos, which had revolted, were destroyed. Papyri place Galerius in Egypt in 293-294, and the Thebaid was soon reorganised with new military commands.
events.debate: Jerome dates the destruction of Busiris and Coptos to 293; some link it to Domitianus' revolt of 297.

events.title: Constantius clears the Rhine delta of Franks
events.summary: After taking Gesoriacum, Constantius swept the Rhine mouths of Franks allied to Carausius and resettled captives as farmers in the depopulated territories of the Nervii and Treveri, a scene the panegyric of 297 describes with captive families waiting in the porticoes of Gallic cities for distribution.

events.title: Maximian's war against the Quinquegentiani
events.summary: Maximian crossed from Spain in 296-297 and campaigned against the Quinquegentiani, mountain tribes of Mauretania who had raided Roman towns, pursuing them into the Atlas; he entered Carthage in triumph on 10 March 298. Rebuilding at Carthage followed, and the campaign secured the African grain supply on which Rome depended.
events.debate: The date of Maximian's adventus at Carthage (10 March 298) comes from a single papyrus/calendar tradition.

events.title: "Pompey's Pillar" raised for Diocletian at Alexandria
events.summary: After the siege of 297-298, the prefect Publius set up a red Aswan granite column 26.85 m high on the Serapeum hill with a statue of Diocletian, honouring him as "the protector of Alexandria" (IGRR I 1068), probably for remitting part of the grain levy to the city. Crusaders later misnamed it Pompey's Pillar.

events.title: Luxor temple converted into a legionary camp
events.summary: Around 300 the Temple of Amun at Luxor was enclosed in a fortress for the legion stationed at Thebes, and a chapel in front of the sanctuary was turned into an imperial cult room painted with life-size frescoes of the four Tetrarchs, among the finest late Roman paintings.
scholarship: Jones and McFadden (eds), Art of Empire: The Roman Frescoes and Imperial Cult Chamber in Luxor Temple (2015)

events.title: Galerius' palace and arch at Thessalonica
events.summary: Galerius turned Thessalonica into a residence with a palace, hippodrome, octagon and a monumental four-way arch whose reliefs depict his Persian victory of 298, including Galerius on horseback duelling Narseh and the capture of the Persian harem; to the north rose the domed Rotunda, possibly intended as his mausoleum and later a church.
scholarship: Laubscher, Der Reliefschmuck des Galeriusbogens in Thessaloniki (1975)
events.debate: The arch is dated c. 298-305; the purpose of the Rotunda (temple, mausoleum or throne hall) is debated.

events.title: Christians purged from the army and palace
events.summary: When the haruspices at a sacrifice in Antioch claimed that Christian officials making the sign of the cross were spoiling the omens, Diocletian ordered all palace staff and soldiers to sacrifice or be flogged and dismissed; the magister Veturius carried out the purge in the army. Christian veterans such as Marcellus of Tingis (298) had already been executed for refusing service.

events.title: Execution of the centurion Marcellus at Tingis
events.summary: At a birthday feast for the emperors on 21 July 298 the centurion Marcellus of the legio Traiana threw down his belt and vine staff, declaring he would serve only Christ; he was tried and beheaded on 30 October. His Acta are an important source for Christian attitudes to military service.

events.title: Mutiny of Eugenius at Seleucia Pieria
events.summary: Some 500 soldiers digging out the harbour of Seleucia, overworked and unable to sleep at night because of the labour, proclaimed their commander Eugenius emperor and marched on Antioch, where the citizens killed them; Diocletian later punished the city's leading men, as Libanius and Eusebius recount.

events.title: Martyrdom of Felix of Thibiuca
events.summary: Bishop Felix of Thibiuca refused to surrender the scriptures under the first edict and was sent to Carthage and executed on 15 July 303, probably the first African martyr of the Great Persecution; his Acta are early and largely authentic.

events.title: The fourth edict: universal sacrifice
events.summary: Early in 304, with Diocletian ill, a fourth edict ordered all inhabitants of the empire to sacrifice and pour libations, renewing the Decian model; it was enforced vigorously in Galerius' and later Maximinus' territories but hardly at all in Constantius' Gaul and Britain.
events.debate: Whether the fourth edict was promulgated in the west is disputed.

events.title: Martyrs of Abitinae
events.summary: Forty-nine Christians, including the priest Saturninus, were arrested celebrating the eucharist in a house at Abitinae and taken to Carthage on 12 February 304; asked why they had disobeyed, they replied "sine dominico non possumus" (we cannot live without the Lord's day). Their Acta were later embellished by Donatists.

events.title: Martyrdom of Agnes at Rome
events.summary: The girl Agnes, aged about 12 or 13, was executed in Rome, probably in 304, and buried on the Via Nomentana; Damasus wrote her epitaph and Ambrose and Prudentius her legend. Constantina built the funerary basilica of Sant'Agnese and her own mausoleum (Santa Costanza) beside the tomb.
events.debate: Date (304 or under Valerian) and age are from later tradition.

events.title: Constantine escapes from Galerius' court
events.summary: Passed over in the succession of 1 May 305, Constantine obtained permission from Galerius to join his father and rode off at night, killing or maiming the post-horses behind him to prevent pursuit (Lactantius, Origo); he found Constantius at Gesoriacum about to sail for Britain.
events.debate: The dramatic escape is a pro-Constantinian story; Galerius probably had little choice but to let him go.

events.title: Constantius' campaign against the Picts
events.summary: Constantius and Constantine campaigned beyond Hadrian's Wall against the Picts, here named for the first time in a panegyric of 297/310, perhaps reaching the far north ("the woods and marshes of the Caledonians"); Constantius died at York on 25 July 306 after the campaign.

events.title: Ascaric and Merogaisus given to the beasts at Trier
events.summary: After defeating Frankish raiders, Constantine had their captured kings Ascaric and Merogaisus thrown to wild animals in the amphitheatre at Trier, and the captives were exposed in the arena, a spectacle celebrated as the Ludi Francici and praised by the panegyrists.

events.title: Maximian tries to depose his son Maxentius
events.summary: In April 308 Maximian, emboldened by his son's victory over Galerius, called an assembly of soldiers and people in Rome and tore the purple from Maxentius' shoulders; the troops sided with the son, and the old emperor fled to Constantine in Gaul.

events.title: Volusianus crushes Domitius Alexander; Carthage sacked
events.summary: Maxentius sent his praetorian prefect Gaius Ceionius Rufius Volusianus with a small force to Africa, which had cut Rome's grain supply; Alexander was defeated and strangled, and Carthage and Cirta were sacked. Constantine later refounded Cirta as Constantina.

events.title: The Aula Palatina at Trier
events.summary: Constantine built a vast brick audience hall at Trier, 67 m long, 27.5 m wide and about 30 m high, with heated floors and a raised apse for the throne, as part of a palace quarter that also included the Kaiserthermen and the double cathedral. Restored after 1945, it is the largest surviving single-room Roman structure.

events.title: Rhine bridge at Cologne and the fort of Divitia
events.summary: Constantine bridged the Rhine at Cologne with a permanent bridge on piers and built the fortified bridgehead of Divitia (Deutz) on the right bank, about 140 m square with 14 towers, garrisoned by the Divitenses; the panegyrist presents it as a yoke on the Franks.

events.title: Maximinus Daia organises a pagan priesthood
events.summary: Ignoring Galerius' toleration, Maximinus appointed high priests for each city and province, dressed in white, with authority to prevent Christians from assembling; he encouraged cities to petition for the expulsion of Christians and had forged "Acts of Pilate" taught in schools. Julian later imitated the scheme.

events.title: The Arycanda petition against the Christians
events.summary: An inscription from Arycanda in Lycia preserves a Greek petition from the people of Lycia and Pamphylia asking Maximinus, Constantine and Licinius to suppress the "atheist" Christians, together with part of Maximinus' Latin reply; a similar rescript to Tyre is paraphrased by Eusebius.

events.title: Martyrdom of Peter of Alexandria
events.summary: Peter, bishop of Alexandria, who had hidden during the persecution and quarrelled with Melitius over the lapsed, was beheaded on 25 November 311 on Maximinus' orders, the "seal of the martyrs" in Coptic tradition. His canons on penance remain part of Orthodox canon law.

events.title: Martyrdom of Lucian of Antioch
events.summary: The scholar-presbyter Lucian of Antioch, reviser of the Greek Septuagint and New Testament text and teacher of Arius, Eusebius of Nicomedia and other "Collucianists", was executed at Nicomedia on 7 January 312 after defending his faith before Maximinus. Helenopolis was built near his shrine at Drepanum.

events.title: The Melitian schism in Egypt
events.summary: While Peter of Alexandria was in hiding, Melitius bishop of Lycopolis ordained clergy in other dioceses and adopted a harsher line on the lapsed, founding a "Church of the Martyrs" that survived into the eighth century; Nicaea tried to reabsorb it, and Melitians allied with Arius' supporters against Athanasius.

events.title: Maximinus Daia's Armenian war, famine and plague
events.summary: In 312 Maximinus fought an unsuccessful war against the Christian Armenians, Rome's allies; at the same time drought, famine and an epidemic with an "eye disease" (perhaps smallpox) struck his provinces, events Eusebius interprets as divine punishment.

events.title: Council of Rome on the Donatists
events.summary: At Constantine's request, Pope Miltiades with three Gallic and fifteen Italian bishops heard the Donatist complaint against Caecilian in the house of Fausta on the Lateran (2-4 October 313), acquitting Caecilian and condemning Donatus; the Donatists appealed, leading to Arles in 314.

events.title: Death of Diocletian at Spalatum
events.summary: Diocletian died in retirement in his palace at Split, embittered by the destruction of his statues and the murder of his wife Prisca and daughter Valeria by Licinius and Maximinus; Lactantius claims he starved himself. He was buried in the octagonal mausoleum, now the cathedral of St Domnius.
events.debate: Date disputed: 3 December 311 (Barnes), 312 or 313; older views 316.

events.title: Constantine rules for Caecilian at Milan
events.summary: After Arles and the inquiry of 315 that cleared Felix of Abthugni of traditio, Constantine himself heard the case at Milan and on 10 November 316 found for Caecilian, ordering Donatist basilicas confiscated.

events.title: Coercion of the Donatists and the Carthage massacre
events.summary: Imperial troops under the comes Leontius and dux Ursatius seized Donatist churches; at Carthage on 12 March 317 soldiers killed worshippers including the bishop of Advocata, events commemorated in the Donatist Passio Donati. In 321 Constantine abandoned coercion and left the Donatists "to God".

events.title: Constantine authorises episcopal courts
events.summary: A law of 318 (CTh 1.27.1) allowed parties in a civil suit to transfer it to a bishop's tribunal, whose decision was final; a later constitution (Sirmondian 1, 333) extended it even to cases moved by one party. Bishops thereby became judges, a role Augustine complained consumed his mornings.

events.title: The Forty Martyrs of Sebaste
events.summary: Forty soldiers of legio XII Fulminata, refusing to sacrifice under Licinius, were left naked on a frozen lake at Sebaste to die of exposure, according to Basil and Gregory of Nyssa; one defected and a guard took his place. Their cult became one of the most popular in the Greek world.
events.debate: Date 320 or 316; details are hagiographical but the core is accepted.

events.title: Licinius restricts the church
events.summary: From about 320 Licinius expelled Christians from his palace, required officials to sacrifice, banned synods, forbade men and women to worship together and ordered services held outside city walls; some churches in Pontus were destroyed. Constantine used this as a pretext for war in 324.

events.title: Pachomius founds the monastery of Tabennesi
events.summary: The former conscript Pachomius, converted by Christian charity to recruits at Thebes, founded a community at the deserted village of Tabennesi c. 323, then Pbow; by his death in 346 his koinonia had nine monasteries and two nunneries with a written rule, shared work and a hierarchy, the beginning of cenobitic monasticism. Jerome translated the Rule into Latin.

events.title: Constantine defeats the Sarmatian king Rausimodus
events.summary: Constantine repelled a Sarmatian invasion under Rausimodus, besieging them at Campona and pursuing them across the Danube where the king was killed; coins with SARMATIA DEVICTA followed. In 323 he chased Goths into Licinius' Thracian territory, provoking a protest that contributed to the war of 324.

events.title: Council of Antioch (early 325)
events.summary: A synod of some 56 bishops under Ossius of Cordoba, meeting at Antioch early in 325 to elect a bishop, issued an anti-Arian creed and provisionally excommunicated Eusebius of Caesarea and two others pending the great council; its synodal letter survives in Syriac.
events.debate: Authenticity of the Syriac letter was doubted but is now generally accepted.

events.title: Constantine's vicennalia in Rome
events.summary: Constantine celebrated the close of his twentieth year in Rome in July 326, his last visit; Zosimus claims he refused to join the traditional procession to the Capitol, offending the Senate and people. The executions of Crispus and Fausta took place the same year.

events.title: Athanasius becomes bishop of Alexandria
events.summary: On 8 June 328, after the death of Alexander, the deacon Athanasius, about thirty and below canonical age, was consecrated by a minority of bishops amid Melitian protests; he would hold the see for 45 years, 17 of them in five exiles.

events.title: Arius readmitted by Constantine
events.summary: After submitting an ambiguous creed, Arius was recalled from exile and readmitted at a second session of Nicaea or a synod at Nicomedia (327-328), and Eusebius of Nicomedia and Theognis returned to their sees; Athanasius' refusal to receive Arius began his long conflict with the court.

events.title: Constantine destroys the temples of Aphaca, Aegeae and Heliopolis
events.summary: Eusebius reports that Constantine had the shrine of Aphrodite at Aphaca on Mount Lebanon demolished for its ritual prostitution, the healing sanctuary of Asclepius at Aegeae in Cilicia torn down, and the temple of Aphrodite at Heliopolis replaced by a church, while statues from across the east were carried to adorn Constantinople.
events.debate: Scale disputed: Eusebius cites a few spectacular cases, and most temples stayed open.

events.title: Amoun founds Nitria; Macarius settles in Scetis
events.summary: About 330 Amoun settled on the mountain of Nitria south of Alexandria and Macarius the Egyptian in the desert of Scetis; by the 390s Palladius found some 5,000 monks at Nitria, with bakeries, doctors and a church, and the outlying Kellia, where Evagrius wrote. Scetis produced the Apophthegmata Patrum.

events.title: Constantine orders a church at Mamre
events.summary: Informed by his mother-in-law Eutropia that pagans, Jews and Christians were sacrificing together at the oak of Mamre where Abraham received the three angels, Constantine wrote to the bishops of Palestine ordering the altars destroyed and a basilica built within Herod's enclosure.

events.title: Church of the Nativity at Bethlehem
events.summary: A basilica built at Constantine's and Helena's initiative over the cave venerated as Christ's birthplace, with an octagon above the grotto, was complete by 333 when the Bordeaux pilgrim saw it; its mosaic floors lie beneath the Justinianic church.

events.title: The Bordeaux pilgrim travels to Jerusalem
events.summary: An anonymous Christian from Burdigala travelled overland via Arles, Milan, Sirmium, Constantinople and Antioch to Jerusalem in 333, listing every mansio and mutatio with distances and noting holy sites, including the newly built Holy Sepulchre; it is the earliest surviving Christian pilgrim itinerary.

events.title: Revolt of Calocaerus in Cyprus
events.summary: Calocaerus, magister of the imperial camel herd on Cyprus, proclaimed himself emperor; Constantine's nephew Dalmatius crushed him and had him burned alive at Tarsus.

events.title: Dedication of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre
events.summary: Bishops from the Council of Tyre moved to Jerusalem to dedicate Constantine's basilica on Golgotha (the Martyrium) on 13 September 335, with the rotunda of the Anastasis still unfinished; the feast of the Encaenia became one of Jerusalem's great annual festivals, described by Egeria. The synod also readmitted Arius.

events.title: Constantine divides the empire among his heirs
events.summary: On 18 September 335 Constantine made his nephew Dalmatius Caesar, giving him Thrace, Macedonia and Achaea, while Constantine II held Gaul, Spain and Britain, Constans Italy, Africa and Pannonia, and Constantius II the east; another nephew, Hannibalianus, became "King of Kings" over Armenia and the Pontic peoples, a calculated affront to Persia.

events.title: Constantine's tricennalia
events.summary: On 25 July 336 Constantine became the first emperor since Augustus to reign thirty years; Eusebius delivered his Tricennial Oration in the palace, setting out the theory of the emperor as image of the divine Logos ruling a world empire mirroring heaven. Constantius II married a daughter of Julius Constantius the same year.

events.title: The three sons of Constantine become Augusti
events.summary: After the massacre of their cousins, Constantine II, Constantius II and Constans took the title Augustus on 9 September 337 and met in Pannonia in 338 to share the empire: Constantine II kept the west beyond the Alps, Constans took Italy, Africa and Illyricum including Dalmatius' share, and Constantius the east and Thrace.
events.debate: Site of the meeting (Viminacium or Sirmium) uncertain.
